Introduction

[
1
]

On October 5, 2022,
Travis Patron was found guilty by a jury of promoting hatred against Jews,
contrary to
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
, RSC 1985, c C-46. This
verdict followed trial on September 26 to 28 and October 3 to 5. This decision reviews
relevant factors in coming to a decision on sentence.

Charge

[
2
]

The Indictment, as
amended, reads as follows:

Travis Patron of Redvers, Saskatchewan
stands charged that he, the said Travis Patron between the 1st day of June 2019
and the 4th day of February 2021 in the Province of Saskatchewan, did by
communicating statements, other than in private conversation, willfully promote
hatred against an identifiable group, to wit: Jews, contrary to
section 319(2)

of the
Criminal Code
.

Sentencing
Principles

[
3
]

Parliament has, in
Part XXII of the
Criminal Code
,
set out the procedure and principles for
sentencing.

[
4
]

Section 718
of the
Criminal
Code
states the fundamental purpose of sentencing as protecting society by
imposing just sanctions that may achieve listed objectives, including
deterrence and rehabilitation of offenders.
Section 718.1
provides that, “A
sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of
responsibility of the offender.”

[
5
]

Section 718.2
of the
Criminal
Code
sets out other sentencing principles, recognizing there are
circumstances that be may either mitigating or aggravating.

[
6
]

Section 718.2(d)
states that “an offender should not be deprived of liberty, if less restrictive
sanctions may be appropriate in the circumstances” and in clause 718.2(e)
directs the court to consider “all available sanctions, other than
imprisonment, that are reasonable in the circumstances and consistent with the
harm done to the victims or to the community …”.

[
7
]

Section 726.1
of the
Criminal
Code
requires the court, in determining the sentence, to consider any
relevant information placed before it, including any representations or submissions
made by or on behalf of the prosecutor or the offender.

[
8
]

Section 726.2
requires the court, when imposing a sentence, to state the terms of the
sentence imposed, the reasons for it, and enter those terms and reasons into
the record of the proceedings.

Circumstances of the
Offence

[
9
]

Travis Patron posted
materials on the internet, including on his personal website (www.travispatron.ca)
and that of the Canadian Nationalist Party, of which he was leader (
www.nationalist.ca
).
These postings included a written document and recorded speech he made titled
“Beware the Parasitic Tribe”.  The recorded speech is under three minutes in
length and of professional quality, with captions of the words spoken.

[
10
]

While the short speech
did not expressly identify the “tribe”, the Crown’s theory was that it referred
to Jews as an identifiable group. The Crown’s evidence, including expert
evidence on antisemitism and antisemitic tropes, supported this theory. The
speech included comments such as “they infect the body politic like a parasite”
and concluded with the statement, “And what we need to do, perhaps more than
anything, is remove these people, once-and-for-all, from our country.” The websites
included other derogatory material that targeted Jews.

[
11
]

These materials, in
particular the speech “Beware the Parasitic Tribe”, generated complaints to
police that resulted in the charge of promoting hatred against Jews. The
complainant who testified at the trial said she found the speech on the
internet in June 2019. The speech was still available on the internet as open-source
material when found by a member of the RCMP in February 2021. So the materials
were on the internet for a lengthy period of time.

Victim Impact

[
12
]

Michael Mostyn, Chief
Executive Officer of B’nai Brith Canada, submitted a victim impact statement in
the form of a letter to the Court. In it he describes “a surge in hatred
towards the Jewish community.” He goes on to say that “Travis Patron’s hate
speech has once against victimized the Jewish Community.  Antisemitism isn’t
just dangerous history, it re-surges again and again. This is deeply concerning
to the Jewish community as dangerous, racist, hateful words can often turn into
dangerous, racist violence.”

[
13
]

The complainant who
testified, Michal Schlesinger, spoke to the impact on her
as a Jewish woman.  She said the speech
was “really shocking to me” and describing the content as “disgusting, such
vile hatred” and that “What stood out … was how he was de-humanizing” a whole
community as parasites.

Personal Circumstances of the Accused

[
14
]

The accused is 31
years old. He graduated from university in 2014 with Bachelor of Arts and
Bachelor of Commerce degrees. He had been living with his parents on the family
farm near Redvers, Saskatchewan.

[
15
]

Mr. Patron appears to
have family support.  His mother and possibly other family members attended the
jury trial.

Criminal Record

[
16
]

The accused has a recent
criminal record.

charge

[
17
]

The complainant who
testified at trial said she found the offending speech in June 2019. So the
materials would have been posted before any of the Saskatchewan offences on
which Mr. Patron was subsequently convicted:
see
2021 SKQB 189
at para
29
. (In that
decision, I upheld the Provincial Court decision to deny bail because of a
pattern of repeated offending and breach of release conditions.)  As such, the subsequent
criminal record is of less significance, aside from indicating an escalating
pattern of offending.

Pre-Sentence Report

[
18
]

There is no
pre-sentence report.

Maximum Penalty

[
19
]

The maximum penalty
for s. 319(2)(a) is two years imprisonment.

Sentencing Range

[
20
]

There is no
sentencing range or starting point established by the Court of Appeal for
Saskatchewan for
s. 319(2)
(a) of the
Criminal Code
.

Crown Position

[
21
]

The Crown proposed a sentence
of one year imprisonment followed by two years on probation on the mandatory
terms, except for an additional term that “Mr. Patron is not to publish or post
on any internet site or any other social media site or platform, where such
postings or publications can be read by the general public, any information
about persons of Jewish religion or origin.” This probation term was
imposed in

R v Topham
,
2017 BCSC 551
at para
60
[
Topham
]
.

[
22
]

The Crown provided sentencing
decisions following conviction under
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
.
None of the decisions are from Saskatchewan.

[
23
]

In
R v Kroeplin
,

2021 ONCJ 19
[
Kroeplin
]
the two accused were found guilty under
s.
319(2)
(b) (a summary conviction offence) for promoting hatred against Jewish
and Black people arising from posters they posted. One poster depicted a Jewish
man and Black man with a rat and cockroach and words drawing an analogy between
them. Another poster showed a Jewish man being bound and shot in the back of
the head. The third poster depicted the flag of Israel inside a target. Neither
of the accused, both of whom were 23 years old, had a prior criminal record.
The Court sentenced both men to a conditional sentence of six months
imprisonment under home confinement followed by two years’ probation and 240
hours of community service.

[
24
]

In
R v Sears
,

2019 ONCJ 607
[
Sears
]
the two accused were found guilty under
s. 319(2)
(b)
for promoting hatred against Jews and women arising from publications in a
community newsletter.  Mr. Sears had a prior conviction for sexual assault. Mr.
Sears, who was in his mid-50s, was sentenced to six months consecutive on each
of two counts for a total sentence of one year. The co-accused, Mr. St. Germaine,
who was 78 years old and in poor health, was sentenced to 18 months’ probation.

[
25
]

Kroeplin
and
Sears
were prosecuted by
summary conviction under
s. 319(2)
(b), so the maximum sentence was six months

[
26
]

In
R v Topham
,

2017 BCSC 551
[
Topham
]
, the accused was found guilty under
s. 319(2)
for
promoting hatred against Jews arising from a website he operated.  The accused
was 70 years old and had no prior criminal record. Mr. Topham received a conditional
sentence of six months with a curfew, followed by two years’ probation. (Since
Mr. Topham was convicted following trial by jury, this charge must have been
prosecuted by indictment under
s. 319(2)
(a).)

Defence Position

[
27
]

Mr. Patron declined
to speak or answer questions at the sentencing hearing.

Other
cases

[
28
]

I reviewed other
decisions involving sentencing after conviction for wilfully promoting hatred
contrary to
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
. Those sentences are
summarized below.

[
29
]

In
R v Dion
,

2020 QCCS 3049
, Downs J.C.S. allowed an appeal against a sentence of 30 days
imprisonment after conviction under
s. 319(2)
(b) and substituted a suspended
sentence with three years’ probation. The offender had made hateful remarks against
Muslims in two YouTube videos.

[
30
]

In
R v Sears
,

2019 ONCJ 606
, Blouin J. imposed a sentence of six months on each count to be
served consecutively for a total prison term of one year.  These were summary
conviction offences, so six months was the maximum term.  Mr. Sears had promoted
hatred against Jews and women over a three-year period in a community
newsletter. (The
Sears
decision
provided by the Crown, summarized above,
although separately reported, appears to be the same decision, except adding
sentencing for the co-accused.)

[
31
]

In
R v Huot
,

2018 QCCQ 4650
, Tremblay J.C.Q. imposed a sentence of 60 days in prison
followed by 18 months’ probation. The offender was 21 years old with no
criminal record and suffered from a severe adjustment disorder with anxiety. While
heavily intoxicated, he had made hateful remarks against Arabs and Muslims on a
Facebook chat following the 2017 attack on a Quebec City Mosque in which
several people were killed.

[
32
]

In
R v Mackenzie
,

2016 ABPC 173
, Fradsham P.C.J. imposed a sentence of five months in jail and
two years’ probation. The offender had spray-painted public and private
property with statements calling for the killing of Syrians.  Mr. Mackenzie had
a recent and relatively lengthy criminal record.

[
33
]

In
R v Castonguay
,

2013 QCCQ 4285
, Decoste J.C.Q. imposed a sentence of 11 months and probation of
three years. The offender had created a website posting degrading and hateful
comments against Jews, Muslims, gays, lesbians and people of colour. He was 30
years of age and had a criminal record for impaired driving, making harassing
phone calls, and possession of child pornography.

[
34
]

In
R v Mahr
,

2010 ONCJ 216
, Douglas J. rejected a joint submission for a conditional
sentence and instead imposed a sentence of six months imprisonment followed by two
years’ probation. The offender had written hateful graffiti on public and
private property on 19 separate occasions over an eight-to-nine-month period.
The writing was directed at Jews, urging others to kill them and promoting
genocide.  The accused, who pled guilty, was 83 years old with no criminal
record.

[
35
]

In
R v Noble
,

2008 BCSC 216
, Parrett J. imposed a sentence of six months in jail followed by
three years on probation, including prohibiting internet access. The offender
had used the internet and created a website to promote hatred against Jews,
Blacks and homosexuals. Mr. Noble was a relatively young man with no previous
criminal record.

[
36
]

In
R v Presseault
,

2007 QCCQ 384
, Vauclair J.C.Q. imposed a sentence of six months and probation
of three years following a guilty plea. The 27-year-old offender had operated a
website for a year on which he fomented hatred against Jews and people of
colour. He was unapologetic and had a criminal record for break and enter,
extortion, concealment, forcible confinement, obstruction of police, conspiracy
and possession of prohibited weapons.

[
37
]

In
R v Ahenakew
,

2005 SKPC 76
,
267 Sask R 124
, conviction reversed
2006 SKQB 272
,
281 Sask R 47
,
affirmed
2008 SKCA 4
at para
15
,
307 Sask R 220
, the trial judge had imposed a
fine of $1,000 after conviction for wilfully promoting hatred by making
disparaging remarks against persons of the Jewish faith in a public speech.  (This
charge was prosecuted as a summary conviction offence.)

[
38
]

In
R v Harding

(2001),
2001 CanLII 28036 (ON SC)
,
40 CR (5
th
) 119 (Ont Sup Ct)
, Dambrot J. dismissed a Crown
appeal against a sentence of concurrent conditional three-month sentences. The offender
had written and distributed two pamphlets with hateful messages against Muslims.
(The decision also dismisses an appeal against conviction, based upon the
statutory defence provided by s. 319(3)(b).)

[
39
]

In
R v Keegstra
,

1996 ABCA 308
,
44 Alta LR (3d) 16
[
Keegstra
]
, the Alberta Court of
Appeal suspended the sentence of one year imprisonment and substituted release
on probation and 200 hours of community service. In doing so, the Court
emphasized that it did so only because of the 12-year delay since indictment,
occasioned by repeated appeals. Mr. Keegstra had promoted hatred against Jews
as a teacher in his high school classes. The majority judgment, at para. 11,
emphasized that “the crime here deserves a sentence of imprisonment”:

[11]
We agree with the Crown that, despite the previous
good record of the accused, the crime here deserves a sentence of imprisonment
in order to express society’s unconditional rejection of hatemongering, to
emphasize the harm to society done by those who preach racial hatred, and to
deter those of a like mind. We agree also that the fact that the accused
promoted hatred to his students in his high school classes over several years
was an aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor. Moreover, when he committed
these crimes, he was not “fighting the good fight”; he was attempting to twist
the minds of young people. And the people of Canada rightly scorn his crime,
and him for never evincing the slightest remorse or regret.

[
40
]

In
R v Lelas

(1990),

1990 CanLII 6836 (ON CA)
,
58 CCC (3d) 568 (Ont CA)
, the Ontario Court of Appeal granted a Crown appeal
against concurrent sentences of six months imprisonment followed by two years’
probation, substituting concurrent sentences of one year imprisonment, for three
counts of public mischief. The offender had spray-painted antisemitic symbols
and words on a synagogue. Although a different offence, the conclusion of the
majority that a more severe penalty was required has since been cited in
sentencing decisions under
s. 319(2)
, at page 575:

In spray-painting the synagogue and
Hebrew school, Lelas was not merely intending to cause damage to property;
rather, to use his words, he wanted "to enrage the Jewish community".
His acts were done to strike fear and terror and to cause emotional upset in
the Jewish community. When mischief is racially or religiously motivated and is
done to cause emotional injury or shock to a particular segment of Canadian
society, it calls for a far more severe penalty than mischief which is done
merely to damage property.

A sentence of six months is not, in my
opinion, sufficient to meet the needs of general deterrence and to show society’s
abhorrence of the acts of the respondent. If it were not for the fact that
Lelas has been released and must be reincarcerated, I would have imposed a
longer sentence. The message must go out loud and clear that conduct, such as
that engaged in by the respondent, will not be tolerated in Canadian society,
and if it is engaged in, it will be met with a severe penalty. Accordingly, I
would allow the appeal, and increase the sentence to one year concurrent on
each count. The probation order should stand. If the Crown requests it, a
warrant may issue for the arrest of the respondent.

[
41
]

From these decisions
and those referred to by the Crown, I conclude that a custodial sentence will
normally follow conviction under
s. 319(2)
(a). A non-custodial sentence may be
appropriate for less serious offences, such as where there is no prior criminal
record, the offender was very young or very old, or the offence was isolated
and impetuous rather than planned.  However, in those cases, the Crown may
proceed by summary conviction under
s. 319(2)
(b). It is the serious nature of
the offence, rather than the circumstances of the individual, that will
generally support a custodial sentence.

Nature of the Offence

[
42
]

Parliament’s concern
with hate crimes is evidenced in the
Criminal Code
, including in
s.
718.2
(a)(i), which provides that evidence the offence was motivated by hate
based on personal characteristics, such as race or religion, is an aggravating
factor in sentencing.

[
43
]

Wilful promotion of
hatred is a serious offence because it attacks and undermines tolerance. Tolerance
is both a virtue and a basic Canadian value. Deterrence and denunciation are therefore
primary objectives of sentencing for this offence. This position was
stated by Butler
J. in
Topham
at para
38
:

[38]
The nature of the harm and the recognition that the
risks associated with hate speech are always present brings home the
observation that denunciation is the most important sentencing principle in
cases involving communication for the promotion of hatred. Communications which
cross the line into promotion of hatred must be denounced. The sentence must
reflect the danger posed by hate speech and society’s abhorrence of such
communications.

[
44
]

The justification for
the law is found in history where dangerous words promoting hatred against vulnerable
groups, if left unchecked and unchallenged, have led to evil deeds. The horror
of the Holocaust is the ultimate proof of that fact.

[
45
]

This point has been
made in decisions of appellate courts in Canada.

[
46
]

In
R v Andrews and
Smith
(1988),
1988 CanLII 200 (ON CA)
,
43 CCC (3d) 193 (Ont CA)
at 211-213
, leave to appeal
dismissed
1990 CanLII 25 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 SCR 870
, upholding the constitutionality of then s. 281.2 of
the
Criminal Code
,
Cory J.A. (as he then was) wrote in the majority
decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal:

I would
have thought it sufficient to look back at the quintessence of evil manifested
in the Third Reich and its hate propaganda to realize the destructive effects
of the promotion of hatred. That dark history provides overwhelming evidence of
the catastrophic results of expressions which promote hatred. The National
Socialist Party was in the minority in the Weimar Republic when it attained
power. The repetition of the loathsome messages of Nazi propaganda led in cruel
and rapid succession from the breaking of the shop windows of Jewish merchants
to the dispossession of the Jews from their property and their professions, to
the establishment of concentration camps and gas chambers. The genocidal
horrors of the Holocaust were made possible by the deliberate incitement of
hatred against the Jewish and other minority peoples.

It would
be a mistake to assume that Canada today is necessarily immune to the effects
of Nazi and other hate literature. Section 281.2 was enacted only after a
careful and extensive study by the Cohen Committee which submitted its report
to Parliament in 1966. The Committee put forward its position in these words:

Canadians
who are members of any identifiable group in Canada are entitled to carry on
their lives as Canadians without being victimized by the deliberate, vicious
promotion of hatred against them. In a democratic society, freedom of speech
does not mean the right to villify [sic]. The number of organizations involved
and the numbers of persons hurt is no test of the issue: the arithmetic of a
free society will not be satisfied with over-simplified statistics
demonstrating that few are casting stones and not many are receiving hurts.
What matters is that incipient malevolence and violence, all of which are
inherent in "hate" activity, deserves national attention. However
small the actors may be in number, the individuals and groups promoting hate in
Canada constitute "a clear and present danger" to the functioning of
a democratic society. For in times of social stress such "hate" could
mushroom into a real and monstrous threat to our way of life. Nor does giving
some of these hate promoters a radio or television platform serve any valid
debating purpose. The Committee is aware that radio and particularly television
may expose malice and fraud for what it is, but such a view of affording an
electronic audience to hate promoters does not take into account the effects of
hate arguments and pseudo-facts on uncritical and receptive minds. The
broadcasting of "hate", therefore, whether for news or exposure purposes,
should be carefully disciplined by those in charge. Indeed, the Committee feels
that in recent years some radio and T.V. producers, with the best of
intentions, have been mistaken in their belief that exposure of this kind will
destroy the virus. But whatever the validity of these views they do not justify
giving propagandists a mass platform as if what they had to say was normal
debate on real issues. Plainly it is not.

In the
Committee's view the "hate" situation in Canada, although not
alarming, clearly is serious enough to require action. It is far better for
Canadians to come to grips with this problem now, before it attains
unmanageable proportions, rather than deal with it at some future date in an
atmosphere of urgency, of fear and perhaps even of crisis. The Canadian
community has a duty, not merely the right, to protect itself from the
corrosive effects of propaganda that tends to undermine the confidence that
various groups in a multicultural society must have in each other.

("Report
of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda in Canada", at pp. 24-5.)

The
committee carefully noted that freedom of expression was the cornerstone of the
Canadian way of life and that it should be impeded as little as possible. For
this reason, s. 281.2 eliminates only wilful public expressions of hatred
directed against groups which can be identified by their race, colour, religion
or ethnic origin. The section was carefully crafted to restrain freedom of
expression as little as possible.

[
47
]

Similar sentiments
were expressed in the majority judgment of
the Alberta Court of Appeal in
Keegstra
,
at paras
14 and 17-18
:

[14]           We also
should emphasize that the accused Keegstra is not a harmless eccentric. He
would have us all believe what he claims, and would have us all believe all
manner of hateful things about the Jewish people. He also knew that what he was
doing was forbidden by his employers. But he arrogantly believes that he knows
better than everyone, his employers, the Courts, Parliament, all his fellow
Canadians. There is only one word to describe such behaviour. It is so perverse
that it is evil.

...

[17]
We reject again Mr. Christie’s
persistent attacks on the law that the accused offended, attacks repeated again
during sentence submissions. Promotion of hatred of discreet groups is a crime
in Canada because widespread hatred of discreet groups is the antithesis of
democracy. Democracy is all about the right of every person in our society to
equal respect and dignity. A democracy is not the happiest society for a
zealot, a person who thinks he knows all truth and is so certain of his
knowledge that he would suppress all opposition as wrong and therefore evil. A
democracy is a happier place for a tolerant person, who may have equally strong
beliefs about what is right and what is true but who is willing to treat with
respect those of a different mind, and use only rational persuasion to correct
their thinking. Mr Christie before us commented upon the paradox of a law that,
in the name of free speech, forbids some speech. But the greater paradox is
offered by the argument that the principle of free speech justifies freedom for
those who would end free speech. In any event, there is no great paradox about
a hate law as a bulwark of a free society so long as we keep in mind that group
hatred is the enemy of freedom. When people in society hate a group, they tend
to tolerate scorn and disrespect toward the members of the group, who thereby
become social outcasts and the victims of all manner of indignities, including
the loss of a voice in public debate. In short, although they never go to
prison, the victims of hatred lose their freedom. The hate law seeks to
preserve their freedom The Canadian hate law condemns hatred of groups defined
by race, gender, religion, or ethnic origin simply because in the recent
history of western society these are the kinds of hatred that have led to
persons ceasing to have civil rights in any meaningful sense. It is not, sadly,
a complete list. But it is a list of occasions for irrational hatred that our
society has rejected as essential if democracy shall be preserved. There have
been few charges laid in Canada under this law, but we do not have to look too
far beyond our frontiers to be reminded how easy it is in this age to stir race
and religious hatred to the murderous level that destroys civil society. In
sum, in Canada the right to free speech is not an absolute right.

[18]
We should also emphasize the
difference between freedom of conscience and freedom of speech. In Canada,
nobody can order the accused to cease to believe what he believes. But we can
and do tell him that he has no right to preach what he believes if his
preaching amounts to hatemongering against peoples. On the contrary, the people
of Canada have decided it is a crime for him to preach like that. And he is not
above the law.

[
48
]

And
in
Saskatchewan
v Whatcott
,
2013 SCC 11
at paras
71-74
,
[2013] 1 SCR 467
[
Whatcott
]
,
Rothstein J. for the Supreme Court of Canada wrote:

[71]
Hate speech is, at its core, an
effort to marginalize individuals based on their membership in a group.
Using expression that exposes the group to hatred, hate speech seeks to
delegitimize group members in the eyes of the majority, reducing their social
standing and acceptance within society. When people are vilified as blameworthy
or undeserving, it is easier to justify discriminatory treatment.  The
objective of s. 14(1)(b) may be understood as reducing the harmful effects
and social costs of discrimination by tackling certain causes of discriminatory
activity.

[72]
The majority
in
Keegstra
[
R
v Keegstra,

1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 SCR 697
] and
Taylor
[
Canada (Human Rights
Commission) v Taylor
,
1990 CanLII 26 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 SCR 892
]
reviewed evidence detailing the potential risks of
harm from the dissemination of messages of hate, including the 1966
Report
of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda in Canada
, commonly known as
the Cohen Committee.  The Cohen Committee wrote at a time when the
experiences of fascism in Italy and National Socialism in Germany were in
recent memory.  Almost 50 years later, I cannot say that those examples
have proven to be isolated and unrepeated at our current point in
history.  One need only look to the former Yugoslavia, Cambodia, Rwanda,
Darfur, or Uganda to see more recent examples of attempted cleansing or
genocide on the basis of religion, ethnicity or sexual orientation.  In
terms of the effects of disseminating hateful messages, there is today the
added impact of the Internet.

[73]

In
Keegstra
, at
pp. 746-47, Dickson C.J. found that two types of harm were of a pressing and
substantial concern.  First, he referred to the grave psychological and
social consequences to individual members of the targeted group from the
humiliation and degradation caused by hate propaganda. Second, he noted the
harmful effects on society at large by increasing discord and by affecting a
subtle and unconscious alteration of views concerning the inferiority of the
targeted group.

[74]
Hate speech, therefore, rises beyond
causing emotional distress to individual group members.  It can have a
societal impact. If a group of people are considered inferior, subhuman, or
lawless, it is easier to justify denying the group and its members equal rights
or status.  As observed by this Court in
Mugesera v. Canada
(Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)
,
2005 SCC 40
,
[2005] 2 S.C.R. 100
, at para.
147
, the findings
in
Keegstra
suggest “that
hate speech always denies fundamental rights”.  As the majority becomes
desensitized by the effects of hate speech, the concern is that some members of
society will demonstrate their rejection of the vulnerable group through
conduct.  Hate speech lays the groundwork for later, broad attacks on
vulnerable groups. These attacks can range from discrimination, to ostracism,
segregation, deportation, violence and, in the most extreme cases, to genocide:

see
Taylor
and
Keegstra
.

Proportionality
and Parity

[
49
]

Section 718.2(b)
provides that “a sentence should be similar to sentences imposed on similar
offenders for similar offences committed in similar circumstances”. I have
considered the sentencing decisions reviewed above.

Aggravating Factors

[
50
]

There are aggravating
factors.

[
51
]

Mr. Patron has a
criminal record, as summarized above.

[
52
]

The offence was
planned and deliberate. It was not an isolated, impulsive or transitory act. It
was carried out over a lengthy period through the creation and maintenance of
the websites and creation and posting of offending materials. The use of the
internet adds impact in potential to reach a wide audience, as identified
in
Whatcott

at para
72
.

[
53
]

The offence has
caused harm. Michael Mostyn, Chief Executive Officer of B’nai Brith Canada, in his
victim impact statement, and the complainant, Michal Schlesinger, in her
testimony, both spoke to the real harm inflicted by the hate speech to the
Jewish community. But the harm of this offence is to the entire Canadian
community, since an attack on one member or group is an attack on all Canadians.

[
54
]

In this regard, it is
worth remembering the words of German Pastor Martin Niemoller. Pastor Niemoller
was imprisoned in Nazi Germany from 1937 until 1945 for his opposition to that
criminal regime.  From his experience, he spoke about the need to stand up
against attacks on minorities:

First they came for the socialists, and I did not
speak out—because I was not a socialist.

Then they came for the trade unionists, and I did
not speak out—because I was not a trade unionist.

Then they came for the Jews, and I did not speak
out—because I was not a Jew.

Then they came for me—and there was no one left to
speak for me.

[
55
]

The target of the
hatred was Jewish people. I have regard to the fact that Jews are
disproportionately targeted in hate crimes: see Kundera Provost-Yombo, Cynthia Louden
& Susan McDonald, “Hate as an Aggravating Factor at Sentencing: A Review of
the Case Law from 2007 to 2020” (Department of Justice Canada 2020) at 12 and
46 (
2020 CanLIIDocs 3732
). Mr. Mostyn makes the same point in his victim impact
statement.

[
56
]

Section 718.2
(a)(i)
of the
Criminal Code
provides that evidence the offence was motivated by
hate based on personal characteristics, such as race or religion, is an
aggravating factor in sentencing. The elements of the
s. 319(2)
offence
incorporate those features in wilful promotion of hatred against an
identifiable group.  In other words, the aggravating feature identified in
s.
718.2
(a)(i) is already part of the s. 319(2) offence. So it cannot make the
individual offence worse than it is already.  Parliament is presumed to have considered
that in determining the maximum sentence.

Mitigating Factors

[
57
]

There are mitigating
factors.

[
58
]

Mr. Patron appears to
have led a good life until recent years, when he began to get into trouble.
This appears to coincide with his adoption and expression of odd and extreme views,
some of which were voiced in court proceedings.

[
59
]

There was no
acknowledgement of wrongdoing or expression of remorse, which would otherwise
be a mitigating factor.

Sentence

[
60
]

I find that
deterrence and denunciation are primary objectives. The conviction addresses
that objective in part. Coming as it does from a jury verdict, it represents a
community repudiation and rejection of the hateful speech.

[
61
]

I also take account
of the fact that Mr. Patron has been imprisoned for the past two and a half
years on remand, awaiting trial on this and other charges.  Most of that time has
been credited to other sentences, leaving the equivalent credit of over six months
time served.

[
62
]

Taking all of these
factors and circumstances into account, I conclude that the sentence
recommended by the Crown of one year imprisonment is appropriate; however, I
will limit the following term of probation to one year, rather than the two
years requested.

[
63
]

The purpose of the
probation period is to provide some protection for the community after his
release. So, I impose a sentence of one year imprisonment, calculated as 365
days, followed by one year on probation.

Credit for
time served on remand

[
64
]

Mr. Patron has spent 131
days in jail which the Crown agrees should be treated as time on remand. He
should be given credit for this time with 1.5 days for each day served, so 197 days
will be deducted from his sentence of 365 days, leaving 168 days to be served
(365 - 197 = 168 days).

Victims Surcharge

[
65
]

There is no fine nor
any victims surcharge, having regard to the Supreme Court of Canada
decision in

R v Boudreault
,
2018 SCC 58
,

[2018] 3 SCR 599
.

Terms of Probation

[
66
]

The following
conditions shall apply during your probation:

1.         Keep
the peace and be of good behaviour;

2.
Appear before the court when required to
do so by the court;

3.
You are not to publish or post on any internet site or
other social media site or platform, where such posting or publication can be
read by the general public, any information about persons of Jewish religion or
origin.

Final Comment

[
67
]

Mr. Patron, my hope
is that on release you will return to the right path as a peaceful and
productive citizen and put these foolish and dangerous thoughts behind you. But
that is up to you. If you continue to make trouble for others, you will also
make trouble for yourself.

J.

D.N. ROBERTSON
